page.title: Shaded streets and the slow work of cooling a crowded city
page.text:
Shaded streets and the slow work of cooling a crowded city
The council has spent four years testing whether narrow shade structures can make a crowded market street usable through the hottest part of the afternoon. Early measurements suggest the difference is smaller than residents hoped, but steady enough that the programme will continue into a third summer.
Engineers began with a single block near the transit interchange, where surface temperatures had been recorded above forty degrees on ordinary working days. They installed light fabric canopies, replaced dark paving with a paler mix, and left the neighbouring block untouched so the two could be compared.
What two summers of temperature readings actually showed
Across two summers the shaded block stayed cooler than its neighbour on almost every recorded afternoon, though the gap narrowed sharply on windless days. Researchers noted that the canopies helped pedestrians most between noon and four, which is also when the market is busiest.
Mature trees performed better than any of the temporary structures, but they were slower to establish and needed watering through the first three summers. Planners now describe the canopies as a bridge measure rather than a replacement for planting along the wider avenues.
Why residents noticed the benches before the canopies
Interviews with market traders and regular shoppers produced a result the engineers had not expected. People described the new shaded benches as the most useful change, because they made it possible to wait for a bus or rest between errands without standing in direct sun.
That feedback pushed the council to add seating to every future shading project, even where the temperature benefit was modest. Officials say the lesson was that comfort is judged by whether a street can be used, not by the numbers recorded on an instrument.
The cost question nobody wanted to answer first
Each canopy costs less than a mature tree to install but more to maintain, because the fabric has to be replaced after several seasons of sun and wind. Over a twenty year horizon the planting programme is cheaper, provided enough of the young trees survive their first summers.
The finance committee asked for a maintenance reserve before approving the next phase, arguing that abandoned street furniture damages public support for later projects. That reserve is now written into the programme budget and reviewed at the end of each summer.
What happens to the shading programme next summer
Two more market streets will be shaded before June, and the council intends to publish its temperature readings so residents can check the claims themselves. The planting programme continues in parallel, with the first avenue trees expected to provide useful shade near the end of the decade.

page.title: Artificial intelligence
page.text:
Artificial intelligence is the capability of computational systems to perform tasks that people usually associate with human intelligence, among them learning, reasoning, problem solving, perception and the making of decisions under real uncertainty.[1]
The field of research sits between engineering, mathematics and computer science, and it develops the methods and the software that let a machine perceive its environment and use what it learns from that environment to pursue goals defined for it.[2]
Some of the most visible applications today include advanced web search engines, the recommendation systems used by streaming services, conversational assistants that understand ordinary speech, and vehicles that drive themselves along public roads.[3]
General intelligence, meaning a machine able to complete any task a person can complete at least as well as the person can, remains one of the declared long term goals of the field and is not considered close by most researchers now working in it.[4]
The discipline was founded as an academic subject in nineteen fifty six at a summer workshop, and it has since passed through several long cycles of considerable optimism followed by disappointment and by the withdrawal of most research funding.[5]
Funding and public interest rose sharply again after two thousand and twelve, when deep learning began to outperform every earlier technique on the standard benchmarks for recognising images and for transcribing recorded human speech into text.[6]
Reasoning, the representation of knowledge, planning, the processing of natural language, perception and support for robotics are among the traditional goals into which academic research in the field has been divided for several decades now.[7]
Researchers have adapted a wide range of techniques in order to reach those goals, including search and mathematical optimisation, formal logic, artificial neural networks, and methods originally drawn from statistics, probability and economics.[8]
Neural networks learn by adjusting the strength of the connections between their many units, so that the network as a whole gradually produces outputs that lie closer to the examples it has been shown repeatedly during its training procedure.[9]
Training a modern model of this kind requires very large quantities of text or images, together with an amount of computing power that only a fairly small number of organisations anywhere are currently in a position to be able to afford at all.[10]
The energy and the water needed to run the data centres involved has become a subject of public debate in several countries, alongside unresolved questions about where the original training material came from and who was asked about its use.[11]
Regulators in several jurisdictions have begun to draft rules covering transparency, the explanation of automated decisions, and the particular circumstances under which a person may formally object to a decision that was made about them.[12]
Surveys of working practitioners continue to disagree about how quickly any further progress will arrive, and the range of published predictions has stayed remarkably wide for most of the last two decades of work within the discipline itself.[13]
